new_statements.quote: Die Opposition Hochton vs. Tiefton ist Halme zufolge ein inhärentes Merkmal des Lexems. Mit Hilfe dieser Binarität kann sie zeigen, dass – entgegen Aussagen anderer Autoren – in einigen wenigen Fällen Minimalpaare in der Nominal- und Verbalsemantik existieren: ila (L) vs. ila (H) 'go for' vs. 'fetch'. [p. 2, <7>] ... Die etwa 6.000 Einträge repräsentieren – im Gegensatz zu den von Halme beschriebenen regelmäßigen und ableitbaren Merkmalen des grammatischen Tons in der Oberflächenstruktur – die lexikalisch gebundene und entsprechend unvorhersagbare tonale Ebene. [p. 3, <10>]
new_statements.translation: The opposition high tone vs. low tone is, according to Halme, an inherent feature of the lexeme. With this binarity she can show that – contrary to statements by other authors – in a few cases minimal pairs exist in nominal and verbal semantics: ila (L) vs. ila (H) 'go for' vs. 'fetch'. ... The roughly 6,000 entries represent – in contrast to the regular and derivable features of grammatical tone in the surface structure described by Halme – the lexically bound and correspondingly unpredictable tonal level.

new_statements.identity_note: Halme 2004 describes Kwanyama as spoken in southern Angola and Namibia (the author lived in a Kwanyama-speaking community in Angola, per the publisher description) and, per Otten's review, compares it with the neighbouring Wambo varieties Mbadja/'Mbandja' and Ndonga, which are treated as separate languages. Tönjes 1910 describes the Osikuanjama of the Rhenish Mission's Ovamboland field (German South West Africa era), per the Wörterbuch preface. Scruggs 1980 is, by its SIL abstract, an overview of common features of African languages, not a Kwanyama-specific description.

new_statements.quote: The present book is the first sketch of Kwanyama grammar with a systematic account on tone. The main aim is to provide an analysis of the tonal system of this language. Therefore the study discusses both the lexical tone, i.e. tone as an inherent property of a lexeme, and the grammatical tone wich marks grammatical properties. [...] As a researcher she keeps to the tradition of Generative Phonology in the sense that there are rules that take the tone patterns from the underlying representation to a binary surface representation, i.e. tonemes.

new_statements.quote: [p. 7] Die Betonung. Als Hauptregel gilt, daß der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe ruht. Daraus folgt, daß bei den einsilbigen Nominal- und Verbalstämmen die vorhergehende Silbe denselben erhält. [p. 8] Bei allen zweisilbigen Nominal- und Verbalstämmen liegt der Ton auf der Stammsilbe; z. B. omufita Hirte ... okudenga schlagen ... [p. 9] Bei den dreisilbigen Stämmen liegt der Starkton, abweichend von der Hauptregel, auf der Stammsilbe und ein Nebenton auf der vorletzten; z. B. omutaleli Aufseher ... okudimbuka aufhören ... new_statements.translation: [p. 7] Stress. The main rule is that the stress rests on the penultimate syllable. It follows that with monosyllabic nominal and verbal stems the preceding syllable receives it. [p. 8] In all disyllabic nominal and verbal stems the stress lies on the stem syllable; e.g. omufita 'herdsman' ... okudenga 'to beat' ... [p. 9] In trisyllabic stems the strong stress lies, deviating from the main rule, on the stem syllable, with a secondary stress on the penult; e.g. omutaleli 'overseer' ... okudimbuka 'to stop' ... The four- and more-syllabic nominal and verbal stems always have the main stress on the penult and a secondary stress on the stem syllable; okuhambelela 'to praise'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress ('Ton', 'Starkton/Hauptton' = dynamic stress; Tönjes explicitly separates it from 'musikalischer Hochton', musical high pitch, p. 10) falls on the penultimate syllable as the main rule. Monosyllabic stems: stress on the preceding (prefix or subject-concord) syllable, i.e. the penult (omunu, efo, ombua; otava fe, ohatu li); prefix ou- always stressed on o. Disyllabic stems: stress on the stem-initial syllable = penult (omufita, okudenga); same for disyllabic adverbs, conjunctions, prepositions, pronouns. Trisyllabic stems: main stress on the stem-initial syllable (= antepenult of the word) with secondary stress on the penult (omutaleli, okudimbuka), also the pluperfect of disyllabic verbs (okua dengele); a listed set of trisyllabic stems (okuangala, okuehena, okufifina, okulotoka, okunangala) and all trisyllabic adverbs/prepositions/conjunctions/pronouns keep penult stress. Four-and-more-syllable stems: main stress on the penult, secondary on the stem syllable (okuhambelela, omufitamatui). Enclitics (xo, xe, mo/po/ko, jo, nge, sa, 'lje, uja, and the monosyllabic stems) fuse with the preceding word, which then has stress on its last syllable (= penult of the group); of two enclitics the first is stressed. Negative particles ha, ke, ka always carry strong stress; sentence stress (Satzton) goes to the focused word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nebenton: on the penult in trisyllabic stems (main stress on stem syllable); on the stem syllable in 4+-syllable stems (main stress on penult); a light Nebenton on a monosyllabic subject concord before the tonic syllable (u longe, va konge) and on any word-initial o- standing before the tonic syllable; past-tense subject concord has 'ein Ton von mittlerer Stärke' on its final a (ova longa); negative imperfect/perfect: Hauptton on na, light Nebenton on the final syllable (inava konga); in reduplications the stem syllables have equal stress (okuendaenda).
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic nominal/verbal stems take stem-initial (antepenultimate) main stress instead of penult, except okuangala, okuehena, okufifina, okulotoka, okunangala which keep penult; trisyllabic adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and pronouns always penult (mongula, onela, kombada); present-indicative concord always stressed on ta, jussive on na (otava, inava); prefix ou- stressed on o; cl. 1/3 sg. prefix omu-: stress on o if u is not syllabic, else on mu; negative particles ha/ke/ka always stressed; enclitics pull stress to the last syllable of the host. Separately (p. 10) a 'musikalischer Hochton' (musical high pitch) with lengthening marks the final -e of distal demonstratives (ovavenjavē) and an emphatic word-final -e on nouns, adjectives, finite verbs and adverbs (ondjila ilē) — Tönjes treats this pitch as distinct from the stress types; he gives no lexical-tone analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Tönjes describes Osikuanjama = Oshikwanyama (Kwanyama, Bantu R.21), the dialect of the Oukuanjama tribe of Ovamboland (northern German South West Africa / southern Angola), as taught at the Seminar für Orientalische Sprachen, Berlin, from his Rhenish Mission fieldwork; Vorwort p. VI notes the title 'Ovambo-Sprache' is loose and that the book treats specifically the Kuanjama dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Halme, Riikka. 2014. Melodic High in Mbadja and Kwanyama. Africana Linguistica 20(1): 145-161. doi:10.3406/aflin.2014.1028
tone_statements.quote: This paper explores new tonal data on the verb system of Mbadja, an Oshiwambo variety spoken in Angola, and compares it to its closely related Oshiwambo variety Kwanyama (R21). Four melodic High patterns were identified for both Mbadja and Kwanyama, with minor differences between the two varieties. The two most frequent patterns are : one without an additional High on the stem, and one with a melodic High from the second vowel of the stem all the way to the final vowel. ... In Mbadja, High verb stems present a distinct tone pattern in the Polarized forms, the O‑forms (an unmarked form with initial vowel ó‑) and the Negative Present and Negative General Past forms used in main clauses.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H vs L verb stems + 4 melodic (grammatical) H patterns on verbs; Kwanyama ~ Mbadja.

tone_statements.quote: The aim of this paper is to show the linguistically interesting tonal phenomena in Bantu languages which have been found by the author so far. ... In §2 several tonal phenomena concerning nouns (especially, tone variations of nouns) are presented, and in §3 some phenomena concerning the tonal figures of verbs of a few languages are given. The languages dealt with in this paper include: Tonga, Nguni, Sambaa, Sotho-Tswana, Nande, Kikuyu, Kwanyama, Sukuma, Nkoya, Mongo, Herero, and Chaga (Machame).

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. Tönjes 1910 (the catalog's cited source) states penultimate word stress as the main rule, with stem-initial (antepenultimate) main stress in trisyllabic stems; Halme 2004 and the Otten 2006 review (existing statements) analyse Kwanyama as a tone language with lexical H/L contrasts and make no stress statement in the parts on record. The two describe different things: a 1910 impressionistic 'Betonung' account (which itself sets dynamic stress apart from a 'musikalischer Hochton' on demonstrative/emphatic -ē) versus a modern tonal analysis. Whether Tönjes' 'Ton' partly reflects high tone or phrase-penultimate lengthening cannot be decided from his text; the catalog's encoding (classification tonal, penult-stress quote from Tönjes) already reflects both and stands.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three Tönjes 1910 quotations are verbatim in the text we hold at the stated pages. (2) The record is internally split: the 'tonal' kind rested on a publisher blurb and Wikipedia for Halme 2004, while the quoted passage is a 1910 missionary teaching grammar describing dynamic penult stress with stem-initial deviations. Open sources downloaded now (Halme 2006 p.160; Otten 2006 review §2, §7; Elderkin 2006) plus the already-held Hurskainen & Halme 2001 p.399 give first-hand/scholarly open-text confirmation that Kwanyama is analysed as a lexical+grammatical H/L tone language with rightward tone shift; none mentions stress, and nothing found contradicts the tonal coding (catalog precedent: Herero, Fipa coded the same way when an old missionary 'accent' statement sits under a modern tonal description). sources.quote: The present book is the first sketch of Kwanyama grammar with a systematic account on tone. The main aim is to provide an analysis of the tonal system of this language. Therefore the study discusses both the lexical tone, i.e. tone as an inherent property of a lexeme, and the grammatical tone wich marks grammatical properties. [...] As a researcher she keeps to the tradition of Generative Phonology in the sense that there are rules that take the tone patterns from the underlying representation to a binary surface representation, i.e. tonemes.

sources.citation: Halme, Riikka. 2014. Melodic High in Mbadja and Kwanyama. Africana Linguistica 20(1): 145-161. doi:10.3406/aflin.2014.1028
sources.quote: This paper explores new tonal data on the verb system of Mbadja, an Oshiwambo variety spoken in Angola, and compares it to its closely related Oshiwambo variety Kwanyama (R21). Four melodic High patterns were identified for both Mbadja and Kwanyama, with minor differences between the two varieties. The two most frequent patterns are : one without an additional High on the stem, and one with a melodic High from the second vowel of the stem all the way to the final vowel. ... In Mbadja, High verb stems present a distinct tone pattern in the Polarized forms, the O‑forms (an unmarked form with initial vowel ó‑) and the Negative Present and Negative General Past forms used in main clauses.
sources.note: Verb tone; four melodic High (grammatical tone) patterns identified for both Kwanyama and Mbadja with minor differences: (i) no additional H on the stem, (ii) melodic H from the second stem vowel to the final vowel (the two most frequent), (iii) melodic H from the second stem vowel to the penult in one verb form, (iv) H on the final vowel in another; High verb stems (lexical H vs L stems) pattern distinctly in Mbadja polarized forms, O-forms and negative present / general past. Presupposes the lexical H/L system of Halme 2004.
